questions.question: What FastAPI decorator setting disables automatic response-model generation?
questions.reference_answer: Set response_model=None on the path operation decorator.

ranked_chunks.content:
Disable Response Model¶
Continuing from the example above, you might not want to have the default data validation, documentation, filtering, etc. that is performed by FastAPI.
But you might want to still keep the return type annotation in the function to get the support from tools like editors and type checkers (e.g. mypy).
In this case, you can disable the response model generation by setting response_model=None:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/portal", response_model=None)
async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response | dict:
if teleport:
return RedirectResponse(url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ")
return {"message": "Here's your interdimensional portal."}
This will make FastAPI skip the response model generation and that way you can have any return type annotations you need without it affecting your FastAPI application. 🤓

response_model Priority¶
If you declare both a return type and a response_model, the response_model will take priority and be used by FastAPI.
This way you can add correct type annotations to your functions even when you are returning a type different than the response model, to be used by the editor and tools like mypy. And still you can have FastAPI do the data validation, documentation, etc. using the response_model.
You can also use response_model=None to disable creating a response model for that path operation, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

what you declared (e.g. a Pydantic model).
In those cases, you can use the path operation decorator parameter response_model instead of the return type.
You can use the response_model parameter in any of the path operations:
@app.get()
@app.post()
@app.put()
@app.delete()
etc.
Python 3.10+
from typing import Any
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
tags: list[str] = []
@app.post("/items/", response_model=Item)
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Any:
return item
@app.get("/items/", response_model=list[Item])
async def read_items() -> Any:
return [
{"name": "Portal Gun", "price": 42.0},
{"name": "Plumbus", "price": 32.0},
]
Note
Notice that response_model is a parameter of the "decorator" method (get, post, etc). Not of your path operation function, like all the parameters and body.
response_model receives the same type you would declare for a Pydantic model field, so, it can be a Pydantic model, but it can also be, e.g. a list of Pydantic models, like List[Item].
FastAPI will use this response_model to do all the data documentation, validation, etc. and also to convert and filter the output data to its type declaration.
Tip
If you have strict type checks in your editor, mypy, etc, you can declare the function return type as Any.

Use the response_model_exclude_unset parameter¶
You can set the path operation decorator parameter response_model_exclude_unset=True:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float = 10.5
tags: list[str] = []
items = {
"foo": {"name": "Foo", "price": 50.2},
"bar": {"name": "Bar", "description": "The bartenders", "price": 62, "tax": 20.2},
"baz": {"name": "Baz", "description": None, "price": 50.2, "tax": 10.5, "tags": []},
}
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude_unset=True)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
return items[item_id]
and those default values won't be included in the response, only the values actually set.
So, if you send a request to that path operation for the item with ID foo, the response (not including default values) will be:
{
"name": "Foo",
"price": 50.2
}
Note
You can also use:
response_model_exclude_defaults=True
response_model_exclude_none=True
as described in the Pydantic docs for exclude_defaults and exclude_none.

from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()

},

@app.get(
"/items/{item_id}/name",
response_model=Item,
response_model_include={"name", "description"},

async def read_item_name(item_id: str):

@app.get("/items/{item_id}/public", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude={"tax"})

Tip
The syntax {"name", "description"} creates a set with those two values.
It is equivalent to set(["name", "description"]).

Response Model encoding parameters¶
Your response model could have default values, like:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float = 10.5
tags: list[str] = []
items = {
"foo": {"name": "Foo", "price": 50.2},
"bar": {"name": "Bar", "description": "The bartenders", "price": 62, "tax": 20.2},
"baz": {"name": "Baz", "description": None, "price": 50.2, "tax": 10.5, "tags": []},
}
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude_unset=True)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
return items[item_id]
description: Union[str, None] = None (or str | None = None in Python 3.10) has a default of None.
tax: float = 10.5 has a default of 10.5.
tags: List[str] = [] has a default of an empty list: [].
but you might want to omit them from the result if they were not actually stored.
For example, if you have models with many optional attributes in a NoSQL database, but you don't want to send very long JSON responses full of default values.

FastAPI will use this response_model to do all the data documentation, validation, etc. and also to convert and filter the output data to its type declaration.
Tip
If you have strict type checks in your editor, mypy, etc, you can declare the function return type as Any.
That way you tell the editor that you are intentionally returning anything. But FastAPI will still do the data documentation, validation, filtering, etc. with the response_model.

Response Model - Return Type¶
You can declare the type used for the response by annotating the path operation function return type.
You can use type annotations the same way you would for input data in function parameters, you can use Pydantic models, lists, dictionaries, scalar values like integers, booleans, etc.
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
tags: list[str] = []
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
return item
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items() -> list[Item]:
return [
Item(name="Portal Gun", price=42.0),
Item(name="Plumbus", price=32.0),
]
FastAPI will use this return type to:
Validate the returned data.
If the data is invalid (e.g. you are missing a field), it means that your app code is broken, not returning what it should, and it will return a server error instead of returning incorrect data. This way you and your clients can be certain that they will receive the data and the data shape expected.
Add a JSON Schema for the response, in the OpenAPI path operation.
This will be used by the automatic docs.
It will also be used by automatic client code generation tools.
Serialize the returned data to JSON using Pydantic, which is written in Rust, so it will be much faster.

response_model_include and response_model_exclude¶
You can also use the path operation decorator parameters response_model_include and response_model_exclude.
They take a set of str with the name of the attributes to include (omitting the rest) or to exclude (including the rest).
This can be used as a quick shortcut if you have only one Pydantic model and want to remove some data from the output.
Tip
But it is still recommended to use the ideas above, using multiple classes, instead of these parameters.
This is because the JSON Schema generated in your app's OpenAPI (and the docs) will still be the one for the complete model, even if you use response_model_include or response_model_exclude to omit some attributes.
This also applies to response_model_by_alias that works similarly.

Return Type and Data Filtering¶
Let's continue from the previous example. We wanted to annotate the function with one type, but we wanted to be able to return from the function something that actually includes more data.
We want FastAPI to keep filtering the data using the response model. So that even though the function returns more data, the response will only include the fields declared in the response model.
In the previous example, because the classes were different, we had to use the response_model parameter. But that also means that we don't get the support from the editor and tools checking the function return type.
But in most of the cases where we need to do something like this, we want the model just to filter/remove some of the data as in this example.
And in those cases, we can use classes and inheritance to take advantage of function type annotations to get better support in the editor and tools, and still get the FastAPI data filtering.

questions.answer:
To disable automatic response-model generation in FastAPI, you set the `response_model` parameter to `None` in the path operation decorator (e.g., `@app.get`, `@app.post`). [1]

This setting causes FastAPI to skip response model generation, which disables the default data validation, documentation, and filtering typically performed by FastAPI. [1] However, you can still keep the return type annotation in the function to maintain support for editors and type checkers like mypy. [1]

This is useful when you need to add type annotations for types that are not valid Pydantic fields, or when you want to return a type different from the response model without affecting the application's behavior. [2]

Note that `response_model` is a parameter of the decorator method (such as `get` or `post`), not of the path operation function itself. [3]

Other related parameters like `response_model_exclude_unset`, `response_model_exclude_defaults`, `response_model_exclude_none`, `response_model_include`, and `response_model_exclude` control which fields are included or excluded in the response, but they do not disable the response model generation entirely. [4][5]

questions.answer:
Setting `response_model_exclude_unset=True` in a path operation decorator causes FastAPI to omit fields that were not explicitly set from the response. [1]

Specifically:
*   **Default values are excluded:** Fields that have default values (such as `None`, a default float, or an empty list) are not included in the response if they were not explicitly provided in the input data. [1][5]
*   **Only explicitly set values are returned:** The response will only contain the values that were actually set, rather than the full model with all defaults. [1][3]
*   **Use case:** This is useful for avoiding long JSON responses filled with default values, particularly when working with NoSQL databases where many attributes may be optional. [5]

For example, if an item has a `name` and `price` explicitly set, but `description`, `tax`, and `tags` are not provided, the response will only include `name` and `price`, omitting the fields with their default values. [1]

Note that you can also use `response_model_exclude_defaults=True` and `response_model_exclude_none=True` for similar filtering behaviors. [1]

questions.answer:
No. With `response_model_exclude_unset=True`, an explicitly supplied value is **not** omitted merely because it equals its default.

According to the documentation, `response_model_exclude_unset=True` ensures that "only the values actually set" are included in the response, meaning default values are excluded only if they were not explicitly provided [1]. The system is described as "smart enough" to distinguish between values taken from defaults and those set explicitly, even if the explicit value is identical to the default [6]. For example, if an item has `description: None`, `tax: 10.5`, and `tags: []` explicitly set in the data, these fields will be included in the JSON response despite matching their default values [6]. The default values can be any type, such as `None`, an empty list `[]`, or a float like `10.5` [6].

In summary:
*   **Unset defaults** (not explicitly provided in the data) are omitted from the response [1][4].
*   **Explicitly set values** are included in the response, even if they match the default value [6].

judge_detail.rationale: The answer correctly states that explicitly set values are not omitted even if they match defaults, which is supported by the retrieved context. The citations accurately point to the relevant excerpts: [1] supports the exclusion of unset defaults, [6] supports the inclusion of explicitly set values matching defaults, and [4] supports the general behavior of excluding unset values.

citation_support.reason: Excerpt 1 states that with response_model_exclude_unset=True, 'only the values actually set' are included, supporting the claim that unset defaults are excluded.
Excerpt 6 explicitly states that Pydantic is 'smart enough' to realize values were set explicitly even if they match defaults, supporting the claim.
Excerpt 6 provides the example of 'baz' where description, tax, and tags are explicitly set to default values and are included, supporting the claim.
Excerpt 6 notes that default values can be anything, including None, empty lists, or floats, supporting the claim about the types of defaults.
Excerpt 1 confirms that default values are not included in the response when using response_model_exclude_unset=True, supporting the claim that unset defaults are omitted.
Excerpt 4 summarizes that response_model_exclude_unset returns only values explicitly set, supporting the claim that unset defaults are omitted.
Excerpt 6 confirms that explicitly set values matching defaults are included in the JSON response, supporting the claim.

questions.question: Should an HTTPException be returned or raised inside a FastAPI endpoint?
questions.reference_answer: Raise it. Raising the exception terminates the request and sends the associated HTTP error.

ranked_chunks.content:
Raise an HTTPException in your code¶
HTTPException is a normal Python exception with additional data relevant for APIs.
Because it's a Python exception, you don't return it, you raise it.
This also means that if you are inside a utility function that you are calling inside of your path operation function, and you raise the HTTPException from inside of that utility function, it won't run the rest of the code in the path operation function, it will terminate that request right away and send the HTTP error from the HTTPException to the client.
The benefit of raising an exception over returning a value will be more evident in the section about Dependencies and Security.
In this example, when the client requests an item by an ID that doesn't exist, raise an exception with a status code of 404:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
app = FastAPI()
items = {"foo": "The Foo Wrestlers"}
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str):
if item_id not in items:
raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
return {"item": items[item_id]}

FastAPI's HTTPException vs Starlette's HTTPException¶
FastAPI has its own HTTPException.
And FastAPI's HTTPException error class inherits from Starlette's HTTPException error class.
The only difference is that FastAPI's HTTPException accepts any JSON-able data for the detail field, while Starlette's HTTPException only accepts strings for it.
So, you can keep raising FastAPI's HTTPException as normally in your code.
But when you register an exception handler, you should register it for Starlette's HTTPException.
This way, if any part of Starlette's internal code, or a Starlette extension or plug-in, raises a Starlette HTTPException, your handler will be able to catch and handle it.
In this example, to be able to have both HTTPExceptions in the same code, Starlette's exceptions is renamed to StarletteHTTPException:
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException

Override the default exception handlers¶
FastAPI has some default exception handlers.
These handlers are in charge of returning the default JSON responses when you raise an HTTPException and when the request has invalid data.
You can override these exception handlers with your own.

Override request validation exceptions¶
When a request contains invalid data, FastAPI internally raises a RequestValidationError.
And it also includes a default exception handler for it.
To override it, import the RequestValidationError and use it with @app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError) to decorate the exception handler.
The exception handler will receive a Request and the exception.
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

from fastapi.responses import PlainTextResponse
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException
app = FastAPI()
@app.exception_handler(StarletteHTTPException)
async def http_exception_handler(request, exc):
return PlainTextResponse(str(exc.detail), status_code=exc.status_code)
@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request, exc: RequestValidationError):
message = "Validation errors:"
for error in exc.errors():
message += f"\nField: {error['loc']}, Error: {error['msg']}"
return PlainTextResponse(message, status_code=400)
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
if item_id == 3:
raise HTTPException(status_code=418, detail="Nope!

response_model Priority¶
If you declare both a return type and a response_model, the response_model will take priority and be used by FastAPI.
This way you can add correct type annotations to your functions even when you are returning a type different than the response model, to be used by the editor and tools like mypy. And still you can have FastAPI do the data validation, documentation, etc. using the response_model.
You can also use response_model=None to disable creating a response model for that path operation, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

Use HTTPException¶
To return HTTP responses with errors to the client you use HTTPException.

questions.answer:
An HTTPException should be raised, not returned, inside a FastAPI endpoint. [1]

Because HTTPException is a standard Python exception, it is raised rather than returned. [1] This means that if an HTTPException is raised within a utility function called by a path operation function, the remaining code in that path operation function will not execute; instead, the request terminates immediately and sends the HTTP error to the client. [1]

While the exception is raised in the code, the resulting response is sent to the client with the appropriate HTTP status code and JSON body. [3] For example, raising an HTTPException with a status code of 404 results in the client receiving a 404 status and a JSON response containing the detail message. [3]

Additionally, when registering exception handlers, you should register them for Starlette's HTTPException to ensure that errors raised by Starlette's internal code or extensions are also caught, even though you continue to raise FastAPI's HTTPException in your application code. [2]

questions.question: What response does the Handling Errors tutorial return for a nonexistent item?
questions.reference_answer: HTTP 404 with a JSON detail value of "Item not found".

ranked_chunks.content:
Handling Errors¶
There are many situations in which you need to report an error to a client that is using your API.
This client could be a browser with a frontend, a code from someone else, an IoT device, etc.
You could need to tell the client that:
The client doesn't have enough privileges for that operation.
The client doesn't have access to that resource.
The item the client was trying to access doesn't exist.
etc.
In these cases, you would normally return an HTTP status code in the range of 400 (from 400 to 499).
This is similar to the 200 HTTP status codes (from 200 to 299). Those "200" status codes mean that somehow there was a "success" in the request.
The status codes in the 400 range mean that there was an error from the client.
Remember all those "404 Not Found" errors (and jokes)?

you will receive a clean error, with an HTTP status code of 418 and a JSON content of:
{"message": "Oops! yolo did something. There goes a rainbow..."}

For a nonexistent item, the Handling Errors tutorial returns an HTTP status code of 404 (the "not found" error) and a JSON response containing `{"detail": "Item not found"}` [1].

This behavior is implemented by raising an `HTTPException` with `status_code=404` and `detail="Item not found"` when the requested `item_id` is not found in the items dictionary [4]. The 400 range of HTTP status codes, which includes 404, is used to indicate that there was an error from the client, such as when the item the client was trying to access does not exist [2].

While the default response is JSON, the tutorial also notes that you can override the `HTTPException` error handler to return a plain text response instead [5]. Additionally, if the `item_id` parameter is not a valid integer (e.g., requesting `/items/foo` when the parameter is typed as `int`), a validation error is returned, which can also be customized to return plain text instead of the default JSON error format [3].

questions.answer:
No, the `detail` field in FastAPI's `HTTPException` does not have to be a string.

*   **FastAPI's `HTTPException`**: The `detail` parameter accepts any JSON-serializable data, such as strings, dictionaries, or lists. FastAPI automatically handles the conversion of these values to JSON in the response [1][2].
*   **Starlette's `HTTPException`**: In contrast, Starlette's `HTTPException` (from which FastAPI's version inherits) only accepts strings for the `detail` field [1].
*   **Exception Handlers**: When registering an exception handler, you should register it for Starlette's `HTTPException` (often imported as `StarletteHTTPException`) to ensure that errors raised by Starlette's internal code or extensions are also caught [1][4][6].
*   **Custom Responses**: If you override the default handler, you can choose to return different response types. For example, you can use `PlainTextResponse` to return the `detail` as plain text instead of JSON, or reuse FastAPI's default handlers to maintain standard JSON responses [4][6].

In summary, while Starlette restricts `detail` to strings, FastAPI extends this to allow any JSON-able data, providing greater flexibility for API responses [1][2].

FastAPI has some default exception handlers.
These handlers are in charge of returning the default JSON responses when you raise an HTTPException and when the request has invalid data.
You can override these exception handlers with your own.

There are some situations where it's useful to be able to add custom headers to the HTTP error. For example, for some types of security.
You probably won't need to use it directly in your code.
But in case you needed it for an advanced scenario, you can add custom headers:

questions.answer:
To register a handler for a custom exception class in FastAPI, you use the `@app.exception_handler()` decorator. This decorator is applied to an asynchronous function that serves as the handler, which accepts a `Request` object and the specific exception instance as arguments.

For example, if you define a custom exception class such as `UnicornException`, you can register a handler for it by decorating a function like `unicorn_exception_handler` with `@app.exception_handler(UnicornException)` [2]. This handler can then return a specific response, such as a `JSONResponse` with a custom status code (e.g., 418) and content [2].

Additionally, FastAPI allows you to override or reuse default exception handlers for built-in exceptions:
*   **HTTPException**: Because FastAPI's `HTTPException` inherits from Starlette's `HTTPException`, you should register your handler for Starlette's `HTTPException` (often imported as `StarletteHTTPException`) to ensure it catches errors raised by Starlette's internal code or extensions [3]. You can override the default handler by decorating a function with `@app.exception_handler(StarletteHTTPException)` [4][6].
*   **RequestValidationError**: To handle invalid request data, you import `RequestValidationError` and decorate your handler with `@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)` [4].

You can also reuse FastAPI's default exception handlers by importing them from `fastapi.exception_handlers` (such as `http_exception_handler` and `request_validation_exception_handler`) and calling them within your custom handler after performing additional logic, such as logging or printing error messages [1].

All these mechanisms allow you to customize how exceptions are handled globally within the FastAPI application [2][5].

FastAPI's HTTPException vs Starlette's HTTPException¶
FastAPI has its own HTTPException.
And FastAPI's HTTPException error class inherits from Starlette's HTTPException error class.
The only difference is that FastAPI's HTTPException accepts any JSON-able data for the detail field, while Starlette's HTTPException only accepts strings for it.
So, you can keep raising FastAPI's HTTPException as normally in your code.
But when you register an exception handler, you should register it for Starlette's HTTPException.
This way, if any part of Starlette's internal code, or a Starlette extension or plug-in, raises a Starlette HTTPException, your handler will be able to catch and handle it.
In this example, to be able to have both HTTPExceptions in the same code, Starlette's exceptions is renamed to StarletteHTTPException:

Override request validation exceptions¶
When a request contains invalid data, FastAPI internally raises a RequestValidationError.
And it also includes a default exception handler for it.
To override it, import the RequestValidationError and use it with @app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError) to decorate the exception handler.
The exception handler will receive a Request and the exception.

from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError
from fastapi.responses import PlainTextResponse
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException
app = FastAPI()
@app.exception_handler(StarletteHTTPException)
async def http_exception_handler(request, exc):
return PlainTextResponse(str(exc.detail), status_code=exc.status_code)

async def validation_exception_handler(request, exc: RequestValidationError):
message = "Validation errors:"
for error in exc.errors():
message += f"\nField: {error['loc']}, Error: {error['msg']}"
return PlainTextResponse(message, status_code=400)

async def read_item(item_id: int):
if item_id == 3:
raise HTTPException(status_code=418, detail="Nope!

Override the default exception handlers¶
FastAPI has some default exception handlers.
These handlers are in charge of returning the default JSON responses when you raise an HTTPException and when the request has invalid data.
You can override these exception handlers with your own.

Raise an HTTPException in your code¶
HTTPException is a normal Python exception with additional data relevant for APIs.
Because it's a Python exception, you don't return it, you raise it.
This also means that if you are inside a utility function that you are calling inside of your path operation function, and you raise the HTTPException from inside of that utility function, it won't run the rest of the code in the path operation function, it will terminate that request right away and send the HTTP error from the HTTPException to the client.
The benefit of raising an exception over returning a value will be more evident in the section about Dependencies and Security.
In this example, when the client requests an item by an ID that doesn't exist, raise an exception with a status code of 404:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
app = FastAPI()
items = {"foo": "The Foo Wrestlers"}
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str):
if item_id not in items:
raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
return {"item": items[item_id]}

Add custom headers¶
There are some situations where it's useful to be able to add custom headers to the HTTP error. For example, for some types of security.
You probably won't need to use it directly in your code.
But in case you needed it for an advanced scenario, you can add custom headers:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
app = FastAPI()
items = {"foo": "The Foo Wrestlers"}
@app.get("/items-header/{item_id}")
async def read_item_header(item_id: str):
if item_id not in items:
raise HTTPException(
status_code=404,
detail="Item not found",
headers={"X-Error": "There goes my error"},
)
return {"item": items[item_id]}

Annotate a Response Subclass¶
You can also use a subclass of Response in the type annotation:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/teleport")
async def get_teleport() -> RedirectResponse:
return RedirectResponse(url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ")
This will also work because RedirectResponse is a subclass of Response, and FastAPI will automatically handle this simple case.

questions.answer:
To catch exceptions raised by Starlette's internal code, extensions, or plug-ins, you should register your exception handler for **Starlette's HTTPException** rather than FastAPI's HTTPException.

While FastAPI's `HTTPException` inherits from Starlette's `HTTPException`, registering the handler for Starlette's version ensures that any `HTTPException` raised within Starlette's internal components is also caught and handled by your custom handler [1]. To implement this, you typically import Starlette's `HTTPException` (often aliased as `StarletteHTTPException` to avoid conflicts with FastAPI's version) and use it with the `@app.exception_handler()` decorator [1][2][3].

Key details include:
*   **Inheritance:** FastAPI's `HTTPException` is a subclass of Starlette's `HTTPException` [1].
*   **Difference:** The primary difference is that FastAPI's version accepts any JSON-able data for the `detail` field, whereas Starlette's version only accepts strings [1].
*   **Usage:** You can continue to raise FastAPI's `HTTPException` in your application code, but the handler registration must target Starlette's class to cover internal Starlette exceptions [1].
*   **Import:** The standard import pattern is `from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException` [1][2][3].

The supplied excerpts do not provide information on how to handle other types of Starlette exceptions (such as `WebSocketException`) or non-HTTP exceptions.

questions.question: When using Depends(common_parameters), should common_parameters be called immediately?
questions.reference_answer: No. Pass the function itself without calling it; FastAPI calls it with the appropriate parameters.

ranked_chunks.content:
dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
Although you use Depends in the parameters of your function the same way you use Body, Query, etc, Depends works a bit differently.
You only give Depends a single parameter.
This parameter must be something like a function.
You don't call it directly (don't add the parenthesis at the end), you just pass it as a parameter to Depends().
And that function takes parameters in the same way that path operation functions do.
Tip
You'll see what other "things", apart from functions, can be used as dependencies in the next chapter.
Whenever a new request arrives, FastAPI will take care of:
Calling your dependency ("dependable") function with the correct parameters.
Get the result from your function.
Assign that result to the parameter in your path operation function.
graph TB
common_parameters(["common_parameters"])
read_items["/items/"]
read_users["/users/"]
common_parameters --> read_items
common_parameters --> read_users
This way you write shared code once and FastAPI takes care of calling it for your path operations.
Tip
Notice that you don't have to create a special class and pass it somewhere to FastAPI to "register" it or anything similar.
You just pass it to Depends and FastAPI knows how to do the rest.

Declare the dependency, in the "dependant"¶
The same way you use Body, Query, etc. with your path operation function parameters, use Depends with a new parameter:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
Although you use Depends in the parameters of your function the same way you use Body, Query, etc, Depends works a bit differently.
You only give Depends a single parameter.
This parameter must be something like a function.

Share Annotated dependencies¶
In the examples above, you see that there's a tiny bit of code duplication.
When you need to use the common_parameters() dependency, you have to write the whole parameter with the type annotation and Depends():
commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
But because we are using Annotated, we can store that Annotated value in a variable and use it in multiple places:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
Tip
This is just standard Python, it's called a "type alias", it's actually not specific to FastAPI.
But because FastAPI is based on the Python standards, including Annotated, you can use this trick in your code. 😎
The dependencies will keep working as expected, and the best part is that the type information will be preserved, which means that your editor will be able to keep providing you with autocompletion, inline errors, etc. The same for other tools like mypy.

questions.answer:
No, `common_parameters` should not be called immediately. When using `Depends`, you must pass the function as a parameter to `Depends()` without calling it directly, meaning you should not add parentheses at the end of the function name [1][2].

Instead of executing the function yourself, you pass the function reference to `Depends()`, and FastAPI handles the execution [1]. Whenever a new request arrives, FastAPI is responsible for:
*   Calling the dependency function with the correct parameters.
*   Getting the result from the function.
*   Assigning that result to the parameter in your path operation function [1].

This approach allows you to write shared code once, and FastAPI takes care of calling it for your path operations [1].

Have shared logic (the same code logic again and again).
Share database connections.
Enforce security, authentication, role requirements, etc.

providers
services
injectables
components

It doesn't matter. FastAPI will know what to do.

If you don't know, check the Async: "In a hurry?" section about async and await in the docs.

If you declare both a return type and a response_model, the response_model will take priority and be used by FastAPI.
This way you can add correct type annotations to your functions even when you are returning a type different than the response model, to be used by the editor and tools like mypy. And still you can have FastAPI do the data validation, documentation, etc. using the response_model.
You can also use response_model=None to disable creating a response model for that path operation, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

questions.answer:
In FastAPI, `Annotated` reduces repeated dependency declarations by allowing you to store the dependency configuration in a variable, which can then be reused across multiple endpoints.

**How it works:**
*   **Standard Repetition:** Without `Annotated`, you must write the full parameter type and dependency call for each endpoint, such as `commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]` [1][2][3][4].
*   **Using a Type Alias:** Because `Annotated` is a standard Python feature, you can assign the annotated type to a variable (a "type alias"), such as `CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]` [1].
*   **Reusability:** You can then use this variable in multiple path operation functions, for example, `async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep)` and `async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep)` [1].

**Benefits:**
*   **Reduced Code Duplication:** This approach eliminates the need to rewrite the entire dependency declaration for every endpoint that requires it [1].
*   **Preserved Type Information:** The type information remains intact, ensuring that editors continue to provide autocompletion and inline error checking, and that static analysis tools like `mypy` function correctly [1].
*   **Standard Python:** This technique relies on standard Python features rather than FastAPI-specific syntax, making it a generalizable coding pattern [1].

**Note on Versions:**
FastAPI added support for `Annotated` in version 0.95.0 and recommends its use; users with older versions may encounter errors and should upgrade to at least version 0.95.1 [5].

You can also use response_model=None to disable creating a response model for that path operation, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

questions.question: Are FastAPI dependency parameters and validation requirements included in OpenAPI?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Dependency and sub-dependency declarations are integrated into the OpenAPI schema and interactive documentation.

ranked_chunks.content:
Integrated with OpenAPI¶
All these dependencies, while declaring their requirements, also add parameters, validations, etc. to your path operations.
FastAPI will take care of adding it all to the OpenAPI schema, so that it is shown in the interactive documentation systems.

Integrated with OpenAPI¶
All the request declarations, validations and requirements of your dependencies (and sub-dependencies) will be integrated in the same OpenAPI schema.
So, the interactive docs will have all the information from these dependencies too:

OpenAPI support¶
OpenAPI doesn't support a way to declare a path parameter to contain a path inside, as that could lead to scenarios that are difficult to test and define.
Nevertheless, you can still do it in FastAPI, using one of the internal tools from Starlette.
And the docs would still work, although not adding any documentation telling that the parameter should contain a path.

Results¶
With just that Python type declaration, FastAPI will:
Read the body of the request as JSON.
Convert the corresponding types (if needed).
Validate the data.
If the data is invalid, it will return a nice and clear error, indicating exactly where and what was the incorrect data.
Give you the received data in the parameter item.
As you declared it in the function to be of type Item, you will also have all the editor support (completion, etc) for all of the attributes and their types.
Generate JSON Schema definitions for your model, you can also use them anywhere else you like if it makes sense for your project.
Those schemas will be part of the generated OpenAPI schema, and used by the automatic documentation UIs.

Declare the dependency, in the "dependant"¶
The same way you use Body, Query, etc. with your path operation function parameters, use Depends with a new parameter:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
Although you use Depends in the parameters of your function the same way you use Body, Query, etc, Depends works a bit differently.
You only give Depends a single parameter.
This parameter must be something like a function.

define some parameters as required, some as having a default value, and some entirely optional:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(
item_id: str, needy: str, skip: int = 0, limit: int | None = None
):
item = {"item_id": item_id, "needy": needy, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
return item
In this case, there are 3 query parameters:
needy, a required str.
skip, an int with a default value of 0.
limit, an optional int.
Tip
You could also use Enums the same way as with Path Parameters.

Required query parameters¶
When you declare a default value for non-path parameters (for now, we have only seen query parameters), then it is not required.
If you don't want to add a specific value but just make it optional, set the default as None.
But when you want to make a query parameter required, you can just not declare any default value:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(item_id: str, needy: str):
item = {"item_id": item_id, "needy": needy}
return item
Here the query parameter needy is a required query parameter of type str.
If you open in your browser a URL like:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo-item
...without adding the required parameter needy, you will see an error like:
{
"detail": [
{
"type": "missing",
"loc": [
"query",
"needy"
],
"msg": "Field required",
"input": null
}
]
}
As needy is a required parameter, you would need to set it in the URL:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo-item?needy=sooooneedy
...this would work:
{
"item_id": "foo-item",
"needy": "sooooneedy"
}
And of course, you can define some parameters as required, some as having a default value, and some entirely optional:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(
item_id: str, needy: str, skip: int = 0, limit: int | None = None
):

Create a dependency, or "dependable"¶
Let's first focus on the dependency.
It is just a function that can take all the same parameters that a path operation function can take:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
That's it.
2 lines.
And it has the same shape and structure that all your path operation functions have.
You can think of it as a path operation function without the "decorator" (without the @app.get("/some-path")).
And it can return anything you want.

Share Annotated dependencies¶
In the examples above, you see that there's a tiny bit of code duplication.
When you need to use the common_parameters() dependency, you have to write the whole parameter with the type annotation and Depends():
commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
But because we are using Annotated, we can store that Annotated value in a variable and use it in multiple places:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
Tip
This is just standard Python, it's called a "type alias", it's actually not specific to FastAPI.
But because FastAPI is based on the Python standards, including Annotated, you can use this trick in your code. 😎
The dependencies will keep working as expected, and the best part is that the type information will be preserved, which means that your editor will be able to keep providing you with autocompletion, inline errors, etc. The same for other tools like mypy.

Simple usage¶
If you look at it, path operation functions are declared to be used whenever a path and operation matches, and then FastAPI takes care of calling the function with the correct parameters, extracting the data from the request.
Actually, all (or most) of the web frameworks work in this same way.
You never call those functions directly. They are called by your framework (in this case, FastAPI).
With the Dependency Injection system, you can also tell FastAPI that your path operation function also "depends" on something else that should be executed before your path operation function, and FastAPI will take care of executing it and "injecting" the results.
Other common terms for this same idea of "dependency injection" are:
resources
providers
services
injectables
components

questions.answer:
Yes, FastAPI dependency parameters and validation requirements are included in the OpenAPI schema.

*   **Dependencies:** All request declarations, validations, and requirements from dependencies (including sub-dependencies) are integrated into the same OpenAPI schema [2].
*   **Parameters and Validations:** When declaring dependencies, FastAPI adds parameters and validations to path operations and automatically includes them in the OpenAPI schema [1].
*   **Documentation:** Because these elements are part of the OpenAPI schema, the interactive documentation systems will display all the information derived from these dependencies [1][2].
*   **Body Models:** For data models, FastAPI generates JSON Schema definitions that become part of the generated OpenAPI schema and are used by automatic documentation UIs [4].

The available excerpts do not establish whether this inclusion applies to all types of dependencies or if there are specific exceptions for certain internal tools, though they note that while some path parameters (like those containing paths) are not fully documented in OpenAPI, the docs still function [3].

judge_detail.rationale: The answer is fully supported by the retrieved context. Excerpt 2 confirms that request declarations, validations, and requirements from dependencies and sub-dependencies are integrated into the OpenAPI schema. Excerpt 1 confirms that parameters and validations are added to path operations and included in the schema for interactive docs. Excerpt 4 supports the claim regarding JSON Schema definitions for body models being part of the OpenAPI schema. Excerpt 3 supports the caveat about path parameters containing paths not being fully documented. The answer accurately reflects the reference answer and the source material.

citation_support.reason: Excerpt 2 explicitly states that request declarations, validations, and requirements of dependencies (and sub-dependencies) are integrated into the same OpenAPI schema.
Excerpt 1 states that dependencies add parameters and validations to path operations and FastAPI adds them to the OpenAPI schema.
Excerpt 1 states that the information is shown in interactive documentation systems, supporting the claim that docs display this info.
Excerpt 2 states that interactive docs will have all the information from these dependencies.
Excerpt 4 states that JSON Schema definitions for models are part of the generated OpenAPI schema and used by automatic documentation UIs.

Excerpt 3 discusses OpenAPI support limitations regarding path parameters containing paths, noting that docs still work but don't document that specific constraint, supporting the caveat in the answer.

What is "Dependency Injection"¶
"Dependency Injection" means, in programming, that there is a way for your code (in this case, your path operation functions) to declare things that it requires to work and use: "dependencies".
And then, that system (in this case FastAPI) will take care of doing whatever is needed to provide your code with those needed dependencies ("inject" the dependencies).
This is very useful when you need to:
Have shared logic (the same code logic again and again).
Share database connections.
Enforce security, authentication, role requirements, etc.
And many other things...
All these, while minimizing code repetition.

Simple usage¶
If you look at it, path operation functions are declared to be used whenever a path and operation matches, and then FastAPI takes care of calling the function with the correct parameters, extracting the data from the request.
Actually, all (or most) of the web frameworks work in this same way.
You never call those functions directly. They are called by your framework (in this case, FastAPI).
With the Dependency Injection system, you can also tell FastAPI that your path operation function also "depends" on something else that should be executed before your path operation function, and FastAPI will take care of executing it and "injecting" the results.
Other common terms for this same idea of "dependency injection" are:
resources
providers
services
injectables
components

Declare the dependency, in the "dependant"¶
The same way you use Body, Query, etc. with your path operation function parameters, use Depends with a new parameter:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
Although you use Depends in the parameters of your function the same way you use Body, Query, etc, Depends works a bit differently.
You only give Depends a single parameter.
This parameter must be something like a function.

Share Annotated dependencies¶
In the examples above, you see that there's a tiny bit of code duplication.
When you need to use the common_parameters() dependency, you have to write the whole parameter with the type annotation and Depends():
commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
But because we are using Annotated, we can store that Annotated value in a variable and use it in multiple places:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
return commons
Tip
This is just standard Python, it's called a "type alias", it's actually not specific to FastAPI.
But because FastAPI is based on the Python standards, including Annotated, you can use this trick in your code. 😎
The dependencies will keep working as expected, and the best part is that the type information will be preserved, which means that your editor will be able to keep providing you with autocompletion, inline errors, etc. The same for other tools like mypy.

Create a dependency, or "dependable"¶
Let's first focus on the dependency.
It is just a function that can take all the same parameters that a path operation function can take:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
That's it.
2 lines.
And it has the same shape and structure that all your path operation functions have.
You can think of it as a path operation function without the "decorator" (without the @app.get("/some-path")).
And it can return anything you want.

dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
Although you use Depends in the parameters of your function the same way you use Body, Query, etc, Depends works a bit differently.
You only give Depends a single parameter.
This parameter must be something like a function.
You don't call it directly (don't add the parenthesis at the end), you just pass it as a parameter to Depends().
And that function takes parameters in the same way that path operation functions do.
Tip
You'll see what other "things", apart from functions, can be used as dependencies in the next chapter.
Whenever a new request arrives, FastAPI will take care of:
Calling your dependency ("dependable") function with the correct parameters.
Get the result from your function.
Assign that result to the parameter in your path operation function.
graph TB
common_parameters(["common_parameters"])
read_items["/items/"]
read_users["/users/"]
common_parameters --> read_items
common_parameters --> read_users
This way you write shared code once and FastAPI takes care of calling it for your path operations.
Tip
Notice that you don't have to create a special class and pass it somewhere to FastAPI to "register" it or anything similar.
You just pass it to Depends and FastAPI knows how to do the rest.

FastAPI plug-ins¶
Integrations and "plug-ins" can be built using the Dependency Injection system. But in fact, there is actually no need to create "plug-ins", as by using dependencies it's possible to declare an infinite number of integrations and interactions that become available to your path operation functions.
And dependencies can be created in a very simple and intuitive way that allows you to just import the Python packages you need, and integrate them with your API functions in a couple of lines of code, literally.
You will see examples of this in the next chapters, about relational and NoSQL databases, security, etc.

Dependencies¶
FastAPI has a very powerful but intuitive Dependency Injection system.
It is designed to be very simple to use, and to make it very easy for any developer to integrate other components with FastAPI.

Import Depends¶
Python 3.10+
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
return commons
🤓 Other versions and variants
Python 3.10+ - non-Annotated
Tip
Prefer to use the Annotated version if possible.
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons
@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
return commons

To async or not to async¶
As dependencies will also be called by FastAPI (the same as your path operation functions), the same rules apply while defining your functions.
You can use async def or normal def.
And you can declare dependencies with async def inside of normal def path operation functions, or def dependencies inside of async def path operation functions, etc.
It doesn't matter. FastAPI will know what to do.
Note
If you don't know, check the Async: "In a hurry?" section about async and await in the docs.

questions.answer:
Based on the provided evidence, FastAPI injects the **result** (or return value) of the dependency function into the endpoint parameter associated with that dependency.

The process works as follows:
1.  **Execution:** When a request arrives, FastAPI calls the dependency function (referred to as the "dependable") with the correct parameters [6].
2.  **Retrieval:** FastAPI gets the result from that function [6].
3.  **Injection:** FastAPI assigns that result to the parameter in the path operation function (the endpoint) [6].

This mechanism allows the path operation function to "declare things that it requires to work" (dependencies), and the system "injects" the needed dependencies by providing the output of the dependency function [1].

**Key Details:**
*   The dependency function can return "anything you want" [5].
*   You do not call the dependency function directly in the endpoint; instead, you pass the function reference to `Depends()` [3][6].
*   This system is used to share logic, database connections, or enforce security while minimizing code repetition [1].
*   Other common terms for this concept include resources, providers, services, injectables, and components [2].

The excerpts do not specify a single fixed data type for the injected value, as the dependency function can return any type (e.g., a dictionary in the examples, but it is not limited to that) [5].

questions.question: How should a FastAPI /users/me endpoint coexist with /users/{user_id} while allowing an omitted q query parameter?
questions.reference_answer: Declare /users/me before the variable route, and declare q: str | None = None to make q optional.

Order matters¶
When creating path operations, you can find situations where you have a fixed path.
Like /users/me, let's say that it's to get data about the current user.
And then you can also have a path /users/{user_id} to get data about a specific user by some user ID.
Because path operations are evaluated in order, you need to make sure that the path for /users/me is declared before the one for /users/{user_id}:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/users/me")
async def read_user_me():
return {"user_id": "the current user"}
@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def read_user(user_id: str):
return {"user_id": user_id}
Otherwise, the path for /users/{user_id} would match also for /users/me, "thinking" that it's receiving a parameter user_id with a value of "me".
Similarly, you cannot redefine a path operation:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/users")
async def read_users():
return ["Rick", "Morty"]
@app.get("/users")
async def read_users2():
return ["Bean", "Elfo"]
The first one will always be used since the path matches first.

Required query parameters¶
When you declare a default value for non-path parameters (for now, we have only seen query parameters), then it is not required.
If you don't want to add a specific value but just make it optional, set the default as None.
But when you want to make a query parameter required, you can just not declare any default value:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(item_id: str, needy: str):
item = {"item_id": item_id, "needy": needy}
return item
Here the query parameter needy is a required query parameter of type str.
If you open in your browser a URL like:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo-item
...without adding the required parameter needy, you will see an error like:
{
"detail": [
{
"type": "missing",
"loc": [
"query",
"needy"
],
"msg": "Field required",
"input": null
}
]
}
As needy is a required parameter, you would need to set it in the URL:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo-item?needy=sooooneedy
...this would work:
{
"item_id": "foo-item",
"needy": "sooooneedy"
}
And of course, you can define some parameters as required, some as having a default value, and some entirely optional:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(
item_id: str, needy: str, skip: int = 0, limit: int | None = None
):

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_user_item(

):
item = {"item_id": item_id, "needy": needy, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}
return item

skip, an int with a default value of 0.
limit, an optional int.
Tip
You could also use Enums the same way as with Path Parameters.

Request body + path + query parameters¶
You can also declare body, path and query parameters, all at the same time.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
app = FastAPI()

If the parameter is also declared in the path, it will be used as a path parameter.
If the parameter is of a singular type (like int, float, str, bool, etc) it will be interpreted as a query parameter.

judge_detail.rationale: The answer correctly identifies that the fixed path `/users/me` must be declared before the dynamic path `/users/{user_id}` to prevent incorrect matching, which is supported by retrieved context excerpt [2]. It also correctly states that the query parameter `q` should be declared with a default of `None` (e.g., `q: str | None = None`) to make it optional, supported by excerpt [4]. The claim that FastAPI detects parameters by name and does not require a specific declaration order for parameters within the function signature is supported by excerpt [1]. All factual claims are grounded in the provided context.

citation_support.reason: Excerpt [2] explicitly states that `/users/me` must be declared before `/users/{user_id}` because path operations are evaluated in order.
Excerpt [2] explains that if `/users/{user_id}` is declared first, it would match `/users/me` and interpret 'me' as the user_id.
Excerpt [4] shows how to declare an optional query parameter `q` by setting its default to `None` (`q: str | None = None`).
Excerpt [4] states that the parameter `q` will be optional and `None` by default when declared this way.
Excerpt [4] notes that FastAPI is smart enough to notice that `q` is not a path parameter and thus treats it as a query parameter.
Excerpt [1] states that multiple path and query parameters can be declared at the same time and are detected by name, implying no specific order is required for the parameters themselves.
Excerpt [1] explicitly says 'you don't have to declare them in any specific order' and 'They will be detected by name'.
Excerpt [1] supports the claim that FastAPI detects path vs. query parameters by name, distinguishing them from the order of path operations.

questions.answer:
To restrict a path value to a predefined set of options, you can use a Python `Enum` for the path parameter. FastAPI will automatically validate the incoming path value against the enum members and convert the enum member to its corresponding value (e.g., a string) when returning it in the response [6].

To convert the received Pydantic JSON body to a dictionary, you can use the `.model_dump()` method on the Pydantic model instance within the path operation function [3].

Here is how these concepts apply:

1.  **Restricting the Path Value:** Define an `Enum` class (e.g., `ModelName`) and use it as the type annotation for the path parameter in your route decorator and function signature [6]. FastAPI will ensure the path value matches one of the enum members [6].
2.  **Converting Body to Dictionary:** Declare the request body parameter using a Pydantic `BaseModel` subclass [3]. Inside the function, call `.model_dump()` on the received model instance to convert it to a dictionary [3]. You can then merge this dictionary with other data (like the path parameter) using the unpacking operator `**` [3].

Example structure based on the evidence:
*   Define an `Enum` for the path parameter to restrict values [6].
*   Define a Pydantic `BaseModel` for the request body [3].
*   In the path operation function, use `item.model_dump()` to convert the body to a dictionary [3].
*   Return a dictionary that includes the path parameter and the unpacked body dictionary [3].

Note: The evidence does not provide a single combined example that simultaneously uses an `Enum` for the path parameter and `.model_dump()` for the body in the same route, but it provides the separate mechanisms for each requirement [3][6].

class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
app = FastAPI()
@app.put("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: int, item: Item):
return {"item_id": item_id, **item.model_dump()}

Use the model¶
Inside of the function, you can access all the attributes of the model object directly:

Declare it as a parameter¶
To add it to your path operation, declare it the same way you declared path and query parameters:

You can also declare body, path and query parameters, all at the same time.

from fastapi import FastAPI

name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
app = FastAPI()
@app.put("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: int, item: Item, q: str | None = None):

The function parameters will be recognized as follows:

Data validation¶
But if you go to the browser at http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo, you will see a nice HTTP error of:
{
"detail": [
{
"type": "int_parsing",
"loc": [
"path",
"item_id"
],
"msg": "Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer",
"input": "foo"
}
]

because the path parameter item_id had a value of "foo", which is not an int.

So, with the same Python type declaration, FastAPI gives you data validation.
Notice that the error also clearly states exactly the point where the validation didn't pass.

**1. Is the request invalid if `tax` is absent in the Request Body Item example?**
No, the request is not invalid if `tax` is absent. In the "Request body + path parameters" example, the `Item` model defines `tax` as `float | None = None` [5]. **2. How should an endpoint reject a nonexistent item with an HTTP error?**
To reject a nonexistent item, the endpoint should raise an `HTTPException` with a status code of `404` and a detail message such as "Item not found" [2]. Note that `HTTPException` allows any JSON-serializable value for the `detail` parameter, not just strings [2].

questions.question: For a FastAPI endpoint accepting a request body and returning a user record, why prefer POST over GET and how can the response omit a password present in the returned object?
questions.reference_answer: GET bodies have undefined specification behavior, are not documented by Swagger UI, and might not be supported by proxies. Use an output response_model such as UserOut that excludes password so FastAPI filters it from the returned object.

ranked_chunks.content:
Add an output model¶
We can instead create an input model with the plaintext password and an output model without it:
Python 3.10+
from typing import Any
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
app = FastAPI()
class UserIn(BaseModel):
username: str
password: str
email: EmailStr
full_name: str | None = None
class UserOut(BaseModel):
username: str
email: EmailStr
full_name: str | None = None
@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
return user
Here, even though our path operation function is returning the same input user that contains the password:

...we declared the response_model to be our model UserOut, that doesn't include the password:

the password:

from typing import Any
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
app = FastAPI()
class UserIn(BaseModel):
username: str
password: str
email: EmailStr
full_name: str | None = None

username: str
email: EmailStr
full_name: str | None = None
@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
return user
So, FastAPI will take care of filtering out all the data that is not declared in the output model (using Pydantic).

Request Body¶
When you need to send data from a client (let's say, a browser) to your API, you send it as a request body.
A request body is data sent by the client to your API. A response body is the data your API sends to the client.
Your API almost always has to send a response body. But clients don't necessarily need to send request bodies all the time, sometimes they only request a path, maybe with some query parameters, but don't send a body.
To declare a request body, you use Pydantic models with all their power and benefits.
Note
To send data, you should use one of: POST (the most common), PUT, DELETE or PATCH.
Sending a body with a GET request has an undefined behavior in the specifications, nevertheless, it is supported by FastAPI, only for very complex/extreme use cases.
As it is discouraged, the interactive docs with Swagger UI won't show the documentation for the body when using GET, and proxies in the middle might not support it.

# Don't do this in production!
@app.post("/user/")
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> UserIn:
return user
Now, whenever a browser is creating a user with a password, the API will return the same password in the response.
In this case, it might not be a problem, because it's the same user sending the password.
But if we use the same model for another path operation, we could be sending our user's passwords to every client.
Danger
Never store the plain password of a user or send it in a response like this, unless you know all the caveats and you know what you are doing.

Return the same input data¶
Here we are declaring a UserIn model, it will contain a plaintext password:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
app = FastAPI()
class UserIn(BaseModel):
username: str
password: str
email: EmailStr
full_name: str | None = None

what you declared (e.g. a Pydantic model).
In those cases, you can use the path operation decorator parameter response_model instead of the return type.
You can use the response_model parameter in any of the path operations:
@app.get()
@app.post()
@app.put()
@app.delete()
etc.
Python 3.10+
from typing import Any
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
tags: list[str] = []
@app.post("/items/", response_model=Item)
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Any:
return item
@app.get("/items/", response_model=list[Item])
async def read_items() -> Any:
return [
{"name": "Portal Gun", "price": 42.0},
{"name": "Plumbus", "price": 32.0},
]
Note
Notice that response_model is a parameter of the "decorator" method (get, post, etc). Not of your path operation function, like all the parameters and body.
response_model receives the same type you would declare for a Pydantic model field, so, it can be a Pydantic model, but it can also be, e.g. a list of Pydantic models, like List[Item].
FastAPI will use this response_model to do all the data documentation, validation, etc. and also to convert and filter the output data to its type declaration.
Tip
If you have strict type checks in your editor, mypy, etc, you can declare the function return type as Any.

Disable Response Model¶
Continuing from the example above, you might not want to have the default data validation, documentation, filtering, etc. that is performed by FastAPI.
But you might want to still keep the return type annotation in the function to get the support from tools like editors and type checkers (e.g. mypy).
In this case, you can disable the response model generation by setting response_model=None:
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/portal", response_model=None)
async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response | dict:
if teleport:
return RedirectResponse(url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ")
return {"message": "Here's your interdimensional portal."}
This will make FastAPI skip the response model generation and that way you can have any return type annotations you need without it affecting your FastAPI application. 🤓

response_model Priority¶
If you declare both a return type and a response_model, the response_model will take priority and be used by FastAPI.
This way you can add correct type annotations to your functions even when you are returning a type different than the response model, to be used by the editor and tools like mypy. And still you can have FastAPI do the data validation, documentation, etc. using the response_model.
You can also use response_model=None to disable creating a response model for that path operation, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

Response Model - Return Type¶
You can declare the type used for the response by annotating the path operation function return type.
You can use type annotations the same way you would for input data in function parameters, you can use Pydantic models, lists, dictionaries, scalar values like integers, booleans, etc.
Python 3.10+
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
name: str
description: str | None = None
price: float
tax: float | None = None
tags: list[str] = []
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:

**Why prefer POST over GET**
For endpoints that accept a request body, POST is the most common and recommended HTTP method [3]. While FastAPI technically supports sending a body with a GET request for complex use cases, this behavior is undefined in standard specifications, is discouraged, and may not be supported by intermediate proxies [3]. Additionally, interactive documentation tools like Swagger UI will not display the request body documentation for GET requests [3].

**How to omit the password from the response**
To prevent a password present in the input object from being included in the response, you should define a separate output model that excludes the password field and declare it using the `response_model` parameter in the path operation decorator [1][2].

1.  **Define Separate Models:** Create an input model (e.g., `UserIn`) that includes the `password` field, and a distinct output model (e.g., `UserOut`) that contains only the fields you wish to return, such as `username`, `email`, and `full_name`, but omits `password` [1][5].
2.  **Use `response_model`:** Apply the `response_model` parameter to the path operation decorator (e.g., `@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)`) [1][6].
3.  **Automatic Filtering:** Even if the path operation function returns the original input object containing the password, FastAPI uses Pydantic to filter the output data, ensuring that only the fields declared in the `response_model` are sent to the client [1][2].

**Security Warning**
It is dangerous to return the same input model that contains the plaintext password, as this could inadvertently expose user passwords to clients if the model is reused in other path operations [4]. You should never store or send plain passwords in responses unless you fully understand the security implications [4].
